To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dose–responses for CeVD and for heart diseases are sublinear in the dose range from 0 to 1.4 and 0 to 3 Gy, respectively.

(1) The dose–response curve for CeVD is below the LNT curve at doses below 1.4 Gys, (2) The dose– response curve for heart diseases is below the Lnt curve at doses below approximately 2.6Gy, (3) There is no evidence for a radiation risk for CeVD and for heart diseases below 0.7 Gy and 0.5 Gy, respectively.
the risk of heart diseases in the atomic bomb survivors was not linearly related to radiation dose and that the dose–risk relation of cerebrovascular diseases is not well established.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and use of statistical methods to improve the accuracy of dose–response modeling.
the validity of the LNT model for cardiovascular diseases in the low-dose and moderate-dose range.
the question whether the linear no-thres- hold (LNT) dose–response model can be applied to radiation-associated cardiovascular diseases (CeVD and heart diseases) at low and medium dose levels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dose–responses for CeVD and for heart diseases are sublinear at doses up to 2–3 Gy, but that the dose–risk relationship is not known at lower doses.
a linear no-threshold relationship cannot be excluded for the dose–response for CeVD and Heart Diseases in the Lifespon Study.
there is no conclusive evidence that radiation causes cardiovascular diseases below a threshold dose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LNT model is not supported for CeVD and is only marginally supported for heart diseases.
the dose–responses for CeVD and for heart diseases are nonlinear, and that the LNT model overestimates the risk for CeVD at low and medium dose.
the LNT model is a good approximation for radiation-associated CeVD and heart disease risks at doses above about 1 Gy, but not below.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of a single model for risk assessment can be misleading and should be replaced by a more robust method that allows risk to be based on a set of models rather than on just a single model of convenience.
MMI provides a more comprehensive characterization and a more accurate determination for the dose–response and a better characterization of the uncertainty.
it is essential to use all available data, including data from epidemiological studies, to derive dose–response models and risk estimates.
